problem_statement.title: CloudFormation: update_stack_instances aborts the whole batch instead of processing each account/region independently
problem_statement.body:
### Environment

- moto 5.2.2
- boto3 1.43.63

### Description

Following up on #10035 / #10041, thanks for adding `StackInstanceNotFoundException`, note this issue builds upon that, there is no regression.

`StackInstances.update()` now raises `StackInstanceNotFound` as soon as it hits the first requested `(account, region)` target that doesn't have an existing instance:

```python
def update(self, accounts, regions, parameters):
    for account in accounts:
        for region in regions:
            instance = self.get_instance(account, region)
            if instance is None:
                raise StackInstanceNotFound()
            instance.parameters = parameters or []
```

`StackInstanceNotFoundException` is a documented error for this API ([`UpdateStackInstances` reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/APIReference/API_UpdateStackInstances.html)), so raising it isn't wrong in isolation. The issue is that raising immediately abandons the rest of the batch, so any targets ordered after the missing one in the `Accounts`/`Regions` lists never get updated, even though they do have an existing instance and should have been. The result depends entirely on request-list ordering, which isn't how AWS documents this operation behaving.

See [StackSet operation options](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/stacksets-concepts.html):

> If a stack can't update in the first Region, the update operation continues in that Region, and then moves on to the next Region.

And the [documented per-instance status codes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/stacksets-concepts.html#stack-instance-status-codes) (`SUCCEEDED`, `FAILED`, `PENDING`, etc.) model each account/Region's outcome independently within a single operation, not as an all-or-nothing, order-dependent result.

### Reproduction

```python
import boto3
from moto import mock_aws

@mock_aws
def repro():
    c = boto3.client("cloudformation", region_name="eu-west-1")
    c.create_stack_set(
        StackSetName="demo",
        TemplateBody='{"Resources": {}}',
        PermissionModel="SELF_MANAGED",
        Parameters=[{"ParameterKey": "Foo", "ParameterValue": "original"}],
    )
    # Only accountA (111...) has an instance; accountC (333...) does not.
    c.create_stack_instances(StackSetName="demo", Accounts=["111111111111"], Regions=["eu-west-1"])

    try:
        # accountC is ordered before accountA.
        c.update_stack_instances(
            StackSetName="demo",
            Accounts=["333333333333", "111111111111"],
            Regions=["eu-west-1"],
            ParameterOverrides=[{"ParameterKey": "Foo", "ParameterValue": "updated"}],
        )
    except Exception as e:
        print("raised:", type(e).__name__, e)

    for i in c.list_stack_instances(StackSetName="demo")["Summaries"]:
        print(i["Account"], i["Region"], i.get("ParameterOverrides"))

repro()
```

### Actual behaviour

```
raised: StackInstanceNotFoundException An error occurred (StackInstanceNotFoundException) when calling the UpdateStackInstances operation: The specified stack instance doesn't exist.
111111111111 eu-west-1 None
```

`accountA`'s existing instance was never updated (`ParameterOverrides` stayed `None`), purely because `accountC` happened to be listed first.

### Expected behaviour

`accountA`'s instance should be updated regardless of the position of `accountC` in the request, and regardless of whether `accountC` has an instance yet. `StackInstanceNotFoundException` seems like the right error for the operation as a whole to surface, but it shouldn't come at the cost of silently dropping updates to valid, existing targets elsewhere in the same request.

problem_statement.title: Path components longer than NAME_MAX (255) succeed instead of raising ENAMETOOLONG
problem_statement.body:
### Description

Path components longer than 255 bytes succeed in the fake filesystem, while the real Posix filesystem raises `OSError: [Errno 36] File name too long` (`ENAMETOOLONG`).

Found by a differential fuzz run comparing the fake filesystem against the real filesystem, so a tested code path can pass under pyfakefs and fail in production.

### Reproduce

```python
import os
import tempfile
from pyfakefs.fake_filesystem import FakeFilesystem, FakeOsModule

fs = FakeFilesystem()
fake_os = FakeOsModule(fs)
long = "a" * 300

fake_os.mkdir("/d")                    # real: tempfile + os.mkdir
fake_os.mkdir("/d/" + long)            # -> succeeds (no error)
os.mkdir(os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), long))  # -> OSError errno 36

fake_os.stat("/d/" + long)             # -> FileNotFoundError (2)
fake_os.listdir("/d/" + long)          # -> succeeds
fake_os.remove("/d/" + long)           # -> FileNotFoundError (2)
fake_os.truncate("/d/" + long, 0)      # -> FileNotFoundError (2)
```

Affected operations seen in the fuzz run: `mkdir`, `makedirs`, `stat`, `listdir`, `scandir`, `remove`, `rmdir`, `truncate`, `rename` (old and new path), `link` (destination), symlink creation and file open — all with an existing parent directory. With a missing parent, the real OS reports `ENOENT`, which the fake already matches.

### Environment

Python 3.13 on Linux; pyfakefs main branch (82ec77a).

# Version

Python 3.13.11
cyclopts 5.3.2

# TL;DR
LimitedChoice doesn't work with boolean flags, pardon my unemployment for this long issue.

# Explanation
I'm currently refactoring the logic of this particular command

```python

import cyclopts
from cyclopts import Parameter, Group
from cyclopts.validators import MutuallyExclusive, LimitedChoice
from rich import print as r_print
from typing import Annotated, Sequence, Any, Optional, Literal


app = cyclopts.App(name="Descartes", alias="dkrt", help="French maxxed CLI for managing task via Markdown tables")


add_mode_group = Group("mandatory flags for additions", validator=LimitedChoice(min=1, max=1))


@app.command()
def add_v2(data: Annotated[
    str,
    Parameter(help="String that is either the path to the .toml file or the list to add")
],

problem_statement.title: toc + attr_list: valueless {: data-toc-label } crashes with TypeError (regression in 3.11.3)
problem_statement.body:
A heading with a bare `data-toc-label` attribute crashes the toc extension: ```python import markdown markdown.markdown("# Hello {: data-toc-label }", extensions=["toc", "attr_list"]) ``` ``` File "markdown/extensions/toc.py", line 124, in unescape return c.unescape(text) File "markdown/treeprocessors.py", line 470, in unescape return self.RE.sub(self._unescape, text) TypeError: expected string or bytes-like object, got 'NoneType' ``` This works in 3.11.2 (it renders `

Hello

`) and crashes in 3.11.3 and on current master. It looks like the same root cause as #1705. Since #1501, `attr_list` stores a valueless attribute as `None`. #1705 fixed this for `id`, but `data-toc-label` is read the same way a few lines further down in `TocTreeprocessor.run()`: ```python if 'data-toc-label' in el.attrib: data_toc_label = run_postprocessors(unescape(el.attrib['data-toc-label']), self.md) ``` so `unescape(None)` blows up. I'd expect a valueless `data-toc-label` to be treated like a missing one: the heading text is used as the label and the attribute is removed, the same as #1705 did for a valueless `id`. Versions: Markdown 3.11.3 and master (4177c1b), Python 3.14.2, Windows 11.

problem_statement.title: RobotsTxtMiddleware shares rules between HTTP and HTTPS with the same authority
problem_statement.body:
### Description

`RobotsTxtMiddleware` caches the parsed robots rules by `netloc` only. Requests to `http://host:port` and `https://host:port` consequently share one parser, even though their robots files belong to different scheme/authority combinations. If the HTTP version allows a URL but the HTTPS version disallows it, the HTTPS URL may be fetched after the HTTP robots file was cached.

[RFC 9309 section 2.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309#section-2.3) identifies the robots file using the URI's scheme and authority. This is about respecting crawler directives, not treating `robots.txt` as access control.

### Steps to Reproduce

Save the following as `repro.py` and run each command in a fresh process:

```sh
python repro.py httpsonly
python repro.py mixed
```

The local server supports HTTP and HTTPS on the same port so the two URLs have exactly the same `netloc`. A temporary self-signed certificate is generated using the `openssl` CLI. All traffic stays on localhost.

```python
import os
import socket
import ssl
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
from pathlib import Path

from scrapy import Request, Spider
from scrapy.crawler import CrawlerProcess

seen = []

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        scheme = 'https' if isinstance(self.connection, ssl.SSLSocket) else 'http'
        seen.append(f'{scheme}:{self.path}')
        if self.path == '/robots.txt':
            data = (b'User-agent: *\nDisallow: /blocked\n' if scheme == 'https'
                    else b'User-agent: *\nDisallow:\n')
        else:
            data = b'OK'
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header('Content-Length', str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)

    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass

class Server(ThreadingHTTPServer):
    def get_request(self):
        conn, addr = super().get_request()
        if conn.recv(1, socket.MSG_PEEK) == b'\x16':
            conn = self.context.wrap_socket(conn, server_side=True)
        return conn, addr

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as td:
    cert, key = Path(td) / 'cert.pem', Path(td) / 'key.pem'
    subprocess.run(
        ['openssl', 'req', '-x509', '-newkey', 'rsa:2048', '-nodes', '-days', '1',
         '-subj', '/CN=localhost', '-keyout', str(key), '-out', str(cert)],
        check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL,
    )
    server = Server(('127.0.0.1', 0), Handler)
    server.context = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
    server.context.load_cert_chain(cert, key)
    threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
    base = f'127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}'
    os.environ['no_proxy'] = '127.0.0.1'

    class Demo(Spider):
        name = 'demo'
        start_urls = ([f'https://{base}/blocked'] if sys.argv[1] == 'httpsonly'
                      else [f'http://{base}/start'])

        def parse(self, response):
            yield Request(f'https://{base}/blocked', callback=self.parse_blocked)

        def parse_blocked(self, response):
            yield {'url': response.url}

    process = CrawlerProcess(settings={
        'LOG_ENABLED': False,
        'ROBOTSTXT_OBEY': True,
        'CONCURRENT_REQUESTS': 1,
    })
    process.crawl(Demo)
    process.start()
    server.shutdown()
    server.server_close()
    print(seen)
```

Actual:

```text
$ python repro.py httpsonly
['https:/robots.txt']
$ python repro.py mixed
['http:/robots.txt', 'http:/start', 'https:/blocked']
```

**Expected behavior:** In the mixed case, fetch the HTTPS robots file and do not fetch `/blocked`, just as in the HTTPS-only control case.

**Actual behavior:** The second case never requests HTTPS robots and fetches the disallowed URL. Each run reproduces reliably in the local test. `robot_parser()` keys `self._parsers` with `url.netloc`, so the HTTP parser is reused for HTTPS. The `SitemapSpider` robots bookkeeping also keys on `netloc` and may need the same origin distinction.

### Versions

```text
Scrapy       : 2.19.0
lxml         : 6.1.3
libxml2      : 2.14.6
cssselect    : 1.6.0
parsel       : 1.12.1
w3lib        : 2.5.0
Twisted      : 26.4.0
Python       : 3.11.0
pyOpenSSL    : 26.4.0
cryptography : 50.0.2
Platform     : macOS-15.0-arm64-arm-64bit
```

Also reproduced from `master` commit `5c7886a3f27dbf8b66f557cc9945dbc4a6aceaac`. Searched open/closed issues and PRs for robots, scheme, netloc and HTTP/HTTPS. Codex assisted with investigation and drafting; both cases were executed locally.

 ## How does HTTP work in Vera?
 
 HTTP is modelled as a built-in algebraic effect. `Http.get(url)` and `Http.post(url, body)` are effect operations that return `Result<String, String>`. Functions that use them must declare `effects(<Http>)` in their signature, making network access explicit and trackable in the type system.

 ## How does contract-driven testing work?
 
-`vera test` is Vera's built-in testing command. It generates test inputs automatically from function contracts — you don't write test cases manually.
+`vera test` is Vera's built-in testing command. It generates test inputs from function contracts, so you do not write test cases by hand.
 
-![Contract-driven testing: Z3 generates inputs satisfying each requires clause, every input runs for real as WASM under wasmtime, and the ensures postcondition is checked against the actual output — a violation fails with the concrete input.](assets/diagrams/contract-testing.svg)
+![Contract-driven testing: for each function the verifier did not prove, Z3 generates inputs satisfying its requires clause, the program is compiled to WASM once and every input runs for real under wasmtime, and the ensures postcondition is checked against the actual output; a violation fails with the concrete input. Proved functions run only under --distrust.](assets/diagrams/contract-testing.svg)
 
 The process works in three steps:
 
-1. **Input generation**: The compiler reads each function's `requires()` clause and uses Z3 to generate concrete values that satisfy the precondition. For example, if a function requires `@Int.1 != 0`, Z3 produces pairs of integers where the first is non-zero — `@Int.1` is the leftmost parameter, since De Bruijn indices count back from the most recent binding. It generates up to 100 trials per function by default (configurable with `--trials`). Whether a parameter can be generated for is decided on its *resolved* type, not its spelling, so an alias of a generatable type (`type Cnt = Int;`) is trialled rather than skipped, and an alias-spelled precondition still constrains the inputs. "Satisfy the precondition" is exact rather than best-effort, for the functions that reach trials at all: among the Tier-3 targets, if any conjunct — or any refined parameter's predicate — falls outside the SMT layer's decidable fragment, Z3 cannot constrain the inputs by it, so the function is *skipped* with the blocking conjunct named instead of being exercised on inputs its own guard would reject. A function the verifier proved at Tier 1 is reported `VERIFIED` and never trialled, so the question does not arise for it — unless `vera test --distrust` runs it too, and then a proved function whose precondition the generator cannot honour is reported `VERIFIED` and not exercised, never run on inputs its precondition does not admit.

 ## What about the training data problem? LLMs have never seen Vera code.
 
 This is a real concern. LLMs are trained on trillions of tokens of Python, TypeScript, and JavaScript. -Vera's approach has three parts. First, the agent-facing documentation (SKILL.md) goes into a model's context window, so the model works from the language specification rather than training data recall. Second, Vera's syntax is deliberately simple and regular (fewer constructs, each with one preferred surface spelling `vera fmt` produces deterministically), which reduces the surface area a model needs to learn. Third, the conformance test suite (programs named by spec chapter and feature) gives models concrete examples to learn from and conform to.  ## Why WebAssembly?
 
-Three reasons. First, portability — the same `.wasm` module runs at the command line and in the browser, which is what the browser-parity suite asserts by running identical module bytes under both hosts; `--target wasi-p2` emits a WASI 0.2 component from that same source. Second, sandboxing — WebAssembly has no ambient capabilities, so a Vera program cannot do anything its effect declarations don't permit. Third, the WASM Component Model (W3C, production-ready in Wasmtime) will enable Vera components to interoperate with Rust, Go, and Python components via WIT interfaces, providing ecosystem access without requiring a massive native package system.

Second, sandboxing: WebAssembly has no ambient capabilities, so a Vera program cannot do anything its effect declarations do not permit. Third, the WASM Component Model (W3C, production-ready in Wasmtime) will enable Vera components to interoperate with Rust, Go, and Python components via WIT interfaces, providing ecosystem access without requiring a massive native package system.

-Correctness over performance. The reference compiler is a specification-faithful implementation, not a production compiler. Python makes the compiler readable, testable, and easy to modify during rapid language evolution. The seven-stage pipeline (parse → transform → resolve → typecheck → verify → compile → execute) is independently testable at each stage.

-Because the whole point is that code should be checkable. If contracts are optional, models won't write them — and then you're back to unverifiable code.  ## Triaging a survivor
 
-1. `mutmut show <name>` — read the mutation.
-2. Classify:
-   - **Weak test** → strengthen it (a discriminating assertion or a new killing test). Same discipline as #680/#734: pick inputs where the wrong behaviour flips the assertion.
-   - **Equivalent mutant** (semantically identical to the original — e.g. `a < b` vs `a <= b` where the boundary is unreachable) → `# pragma: no mutate` on the line, with a one-line rationale.
-   - **Genuine coverage gap** → add a test.
-3. **Re-confirm** (Z3-flakiness guardrail): re-run the specific mutant ≥2× before trusting a survivor. A mutant that makes a verification *barely* unsolvable can hit the Z3 timeout → `unknown` → Tier-3 and survive nondeterministically. If a survivor flips between runs, it's timeout-flaky, not a weak test — raise the `--timeout` / Z3 timeout rather than "fixing" a test.

 ## The measure-all baseline
 
-The whole of `vera/` is measured by the nightly sweep: `.github/workflows/mutation-nightly.yml` running `scripts/mutate_sweep.py` over a random sample of the tree's mutants, a cycle a night or two. No single run holds every mutant, and no cycle tries to. At 874bc7f4 mutmut 3.8.1's visitor makes 113,127 mutants in the 2,486 functions it mutates in `vera/`, and a mutant costs from a twentieth of a second (killed by its first test) to most of an hour on a runner: a survivor runs every test that reaches its function, and a compiler's front-end functions are reached by thousands. The sweep that measured every mutant decided 300 to 1,300 a night over the nights of October 2026, so a cycle would have taken months of green nights against a tree that changes daily, and 9 of its first 18 scheduled nights were red ([#1827](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1827)). The one local marathon that tried, on mutmut 3.6 and Python 3.14, deadlocked four times, 30% to 55% of the way through; the sweep has no marathon, so it does not meet that hang, and its runners use Python 3.12, as the test shards do.

 **A night.** At 21:00 UTC the `setup` job finds the state the last night left: the `mutation-sweep-state` artifact of the newest completed run of this workflow on this repository's own `main`, started by the schedule or a dispatch, that holds one unexpired. A fork's run on a branch named `main`, or another workflow's run, could upload an artifact of that name, so no other run's is taken, and the state is checked field by field before it is used. Seven `sweep` jobs (`JOBS` in the script) then each plan the same night from it and run their slice:
 
-- The inventory: every function mutmut mutates, with a hash of its text, the lines it spans: its mutants are placed by line, and the state numbers its lines from the function's first, so a change inside it (a comment or a docstring included, since either moves the lines below it) starts it afresh, and an edit above it in the file moves nothing. A function gone from the tree is dropped, and a new mutmut version starts every function afresh, since mutmut makes a function's mutants by its own rules.
-- The count: each function's mutants, in all and by the line mutmut places each on (the mutated node's first line, which its covered-lines hook reads a node by; the state numbers a function's lines from its first), counted by mutmut's own visitor through the engine's `count` command (`scripts/mutate_diff.py --as-engine count`, 46 s for the whole tree on the measuring machine, about two minutes on a runner) for the functions the state holds uncounted. Each slice's record carries the counts it made, and the stitch folds them into the state.
-- The sample: a line of a function is in the cycle's sample when a hash of the cycle, the function and the line falls under `SAMPLE_FRACTION` (2%), and the sample is every mutant on a sampled line, so every job of a night and every night of the cycle draw the same sample, each mutant in it with the same chance, and the next cycle draws another. At 2% of about 113,000 the sample is about 2,300 mutants, drawn in the small clusters a line holds, and the whole-tree score's 95% interval about ±2 points; a module's own interval follows its share. The sample is drawn by line because mutmut generates a kept function's mutants whole, every one into the copy: a sample of mutants drawn one by one filled a job with bins of 150 to 200 functions, which spent 30 minutes to four hours generating and compiling the copy before the first pass ran ([#1829](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1829)), where a sample of lines reaches mutmut's generator through the covered-lines hook, as the diff lane's window does, and the copy holds the sample's mutants alone.
-- The plan: the sample's undecided mutants, each function's window (its sampled lines) less the mutants an earlier night decided, the functions in the tree's order while their estimated cost fits the night, the night's jobs times a job's budget (4.5 h) less the passes before its first mutant (`FIXED_S`, two hours: over the fourteen slices of 29 October to 3 November 2026 with a full record, the stats pass took 45 to 130 minutes, the clean run 40 to 70 and the forced-fail run up to 25, each on one core), at an estimated cost a mutant: 25 s in the soundness core and 2.5 s elsewhere, times a factor each night measures from the recorded duration of every mutant it decided. The night's first function is taken whatever it costs, so a night with work open decides something. The functions are then spread over every job of the night, each whole, the dearest first into the job holding least, so each job has work while the functions outnumber them: on the nights of 7 to 10 November 2026 three of seven jobs planned nothing while 362 mutants waited ([#1838](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1838)). One rate per family cannot describe a bin whose undecided mutants are the dearest of their functions, since mutmut runs a bin's cheapest first, so a bin can still be over-planned; keeping each mutant as it is decided is what makes that harmless.
-- The run: a scratch tree of the head, narrowed to the bin's functions as the diff lane narrows a diff's, their sampled lines handed to mutmut as the window (§ CI: the diff lane), so mutmut generates the windows' mutants and no others, each function's numbered `1` to its window's count in the order of its lines. A function's window is fixed for the cycle (its sampled lines at its hash), so a number names one mutant on every night of the cycle, and mutmut is handed each undecided mutant by that name (`vera.verifier.xǁContractVerifierǁ_verify_fn_contracts__mutmut_41`) and no other. The names also set the clean run: mutmut runs clean the tests its stats pass recorded reaching the named functions, where a glob such as `key__mutmut_*`, which mutmut matches against the functions' names, named none and left the clean run to the whole selection, 40 to 80 minutes of each slice on one core. Each slice runs two workers (`--max-children 2`): with four, a bin's dearest mutants, its survivors, ran together at its end and took the runner into swap. The engine counts what it generated against the window, and a listing of more or fewer mutants of a function than its window holds is a stop the night reports. mutmut's copy holds the whole tree, and the oracle is every `tests/test_*.py` file the lane's rule admits (255 of 293 today), the subprocess, Node and tooling families left out. A test that starts a Python or `vera` process, or reads the compiler's source, is no oracle in the copy (§ Oracle); one that fails there with no mutant active is dropped from the run and reported, and every night after deselects it from the start, since a drop costs a stats pass (the pass stops at the failure with nothing saved, and the rerun starts it over; four such drops cost each of four slices its whole budget on 3 November 2026), until the tree no longer holds the test's file. An exception the engine's own code raises stops the slice instead, dropping no further test, and its record and the night's report name the exception and the engine's frame (§ CI: the diff lane, The oracle).
-- The `stitch` job folds the slices' counts and decided mutants into the state, a mutant at a time, and keeps it as the `mutation-sweep-state` artifact for 90 days. A window partly decided keeps its decided mutants (`partial`, by window number) and becomes a decided window when its last mutant is decided. mutmut runs a bin's mutants in ascending order of their estimated cost, across the whole bin, so under the rule that counted a window only when it was whole, the nights of 7 to 10 November 2026 decided at least 201 mutants and recorded 34, and each night decided the same cheap mutants again. +**What it mutates.** The diff from the pull request's merge base, mapped to the units mutmut mutates: a top-level function, or a method of a top-level class, with a nested function belonging to the one that encloses it. A unit counts as changed when its code differs from the merge base's (its `ast`, docstrings set aside) or it is new, so a docstring, a comment or a layout change alone mutates nothing. The script extracts the head commit into a scratch tree (`git archive`; the checkout is never touched) and gives every unit the diff leaves alone in a changed file `# pragma: no mutate block` on its header, so mutmut generates the changed units' mutants and no others.
+
+Inside those units it generates only the window's mutants: those whose node starts within two lines (`--context`) of a line the diff adds, or of a point where it removes lines and adds none, or on the first line of a node that spans such a line and whose mutants mutmut places on that first line though the text they change lies below it. Those nodes are a call (an argument's `None` and its removal, a `dict` keyword's rename, a string method's swap after a receiver of several lines), a `match` (a `case`'s removal), an assignment (plain, annotated or augmented), a binary or boolean operation, a comparison's operator, which starts with the line break before it, a conditional expression and a lambda (`ENCLOSING_KINDS` in the script). For example, an edit to a diagnostic's `error_code="E302",` at `vera/checker/control.py`:430 keeps the argument's `None` and its removal, which mutmut places on the call's first line at :419: the window holds 17 of the function's 143 mutants, where the edit's lines alone hold 5.
+
+The engine is the script itself run with `--as-engine`. It counts each unit's mutants on every line and in the window with mutmut's own visitor, then hands each narrowed file's window to mutmut's covered-lines hook (`get_covered_lines_for_file`, the filter it reads a node's start line against).  #### IO model: terminal vs browser
 
-Vera's "write once, run anywhere" claim has a real seam at the IO boundary, and writing for one target without thinking about the other will produce a program that compiles cleanly to both but only *runs* meaningfully on one:
+The two targets differ at the IO boundary, and writing for one target without thinking about the other produces a program that compiles cleanly to both but only *runs* meaningfully on one:

 `tests/pipeline.py` is the suite's one driver for the compiler pipeline.  It has one function per stage (`parse`, `check`, `verify`, `compile`, `run` and `contract_test`), each of which runs the stages before it in process, wired as the CLI wires them, and returns the stage's result: `ok`, the diagnostics in the order the CLI reports them, the artefact the stage made, and `envelope()`, the object `vera <stage> --json` prints.  A stage takes source text or a path, and a path's imports resolve from its directory, as the CLI resolves them.  Reading an artefact a stage did not make raises what stopped it: the parse error, the trap, or `StageFailed` naming the errors of the stage that refused the program.  `cli()` runs `vera.cli.main` in process for a test that crosses the CLI.  `tests/checker_helpers.py`, `tests/verifier_helpers.py`, `tests/codegen_helpers.py` and `tests/module_fixture_helpers.py` are layers over it. @@ -0,0 +1,23 @@
+- The documents, the specification and the diagrams say what the compiler does.  Each statement a command can check was run against 0.2.8, and about 140 were wrong.  `README.md` said a quantified `ensures` gets no runtime check, where the contract code generation does not lower is an `ensures` on a function that returns a `String` or an `Array`, disclosed as `E543`; `vera verify examples/safe_divide.vera` verifies 9 obligations, not 6; the warnings that disclose an obligation nothing guards are `E504`, `E506`, `E539`, `E540`, `E542` and `E543`; `SKILL.md` said `Tuple<>` is `Unit`, which is a parse error, and `FAQ.md` that `Bool` is `Ord`, which is `E242`; `TESTING.md` now documents the envelopes `vera compile --json` and `vera run --json` print; `MUTATION.md` gave the sweep's state schema as 2, which is 3; and `vera/README.md` named functions that do not exist.
+- The specification no longer contradicts itself or the reference compiler where a sentence was overruled by another section or by what runs:
+  - §2.8 rule 5 states the variance the checker implements: a data type is covariant in its type arguments (`Array<PosInt> <: Array<Int>`), and a function type is contravariant in its parameters and covariant in its result and its effect row (§7.8).  It said compound types have no variance.  Its implementation note says the `Int` to `Nat` relaxation reaches a data type's type argument, so an `Array<Int>` where an `Array<Nat>` is expected is an obligated narrowing of its elements, checked at run time where the verifier cannot discharge it.
+  - §2.6.5 says a refinement's guard is compiled and evaluated even where `vera verify` proves the predicate, and that a program `vera verify` accepts can still hold Tier 3 predicates whose guards are the check.  It said a verified program never reaches the guard.
+  - §5.9 follows §4.2: the type a result is expected at fixes a type argument whatever the literals' signs.
+  - §2.1 says a `let` declares its type, as §4.7 and the grammar do.
+  - §3.7 defines `@Fn`, the name every binding written with a function type shares, and §3.3 and §3.10 list closure parameters and handler state as binding sites.
+  - §5.9.1 and §7.6 bind the effect variable their examples use, so the `E340` they describe is the error the compiler gives.  §5.5 says an effect variable stands only in a function type's row, and a function's own row that names one is refused (`E340`).
+  - §5.4 drops the note it said the compiler SHOULD emit for `requires(true)` and `ensures(true)`, which are the canonical spelling of a function with no precondition and no postcondition.
+  - §6.4.3 says `Int` division carries the overflow obligation for `INT_MIN / -1` (`E528`).  Its table said that case traps with no obligation.
+  - §6.8's table says a refuted Tier 1 obligation is a `vera verify` error, where it said a compile error, and that a Tier 3 site no check can evaluate is disclosed and counted in no tier.  The guarantee of a fully verified program loses the condition "if it compiles", since `vera compile` does not verify.  The conformance program's summary is 9 verified, not 8.  §6.8.1 names the `ensures` with no runtime check as one on a function that returns a `String` or an `Array`, where it named a quantified `ensures`.
+  - §7.2 rule 6 says a qualified call of a user-declared effect's operation outside its row is `E340` and a bare call outside a `handle` block is `E217`, as §7.4 does.  It gave `E340` for both.

 ### When to use recursion instead
 
 Closures cover pure, self-contained transformations and simple captured constants. Prefer a top-level recursive function when any of these hold:
 
-- The body needs an effect row other than `pure` that doesn't match the combinator's expected effect signature.
-- The body needs to early-return or short-circuit in a way the combinator doesn't provide (`array_find` / `array_any` / `array_all` short-circuit; `array_map` / `array_fold` do not).
-- The iteration shape isn't one-pass left-to-right (e.g. you need to look ahead, or process in reverse while mutating a different data structure).

 ### Error codes
 
-Every diagnostic has a stable code grouped by compiler phase — the `W` series is warnings, the `E` series errors:
-
-- **W001** — Typed hole (`?`) — expected type and available bindings reported (warning, not error)
-- **W002** — `async()` argument evaluates eagerly: its effects fall outside the commutative set (`Http`), so the future is computed sequentially at the `async()` site rather than concurrently (warning, not error)
-- **W003** — Unverified assumption: an `assume` statement is taken on trust, not proved (warning, not error)
-- **W004** — `vera verify` found a runtime check in the compiled module that no verification record accounts for: the check still runs, and the summary omits it (warning, not error)
-- **W005** — `vera verify` did not reconcile the runtime checks, because the program holds typed holes and code generation compiles nothing until they are filled (warning, not error)
-- **E001–E009** — Parse errors (missing contracts, unexpected tokens, malformed slot references, bad string escapes)
-- **E011–E013** — Import errors (circular import, unresolvable import, a module that fails to parse)
-- **E020, E021, E023** — Malformed comments: unterminated `{-` (E020) or `/*` (E021), or a `/*` nested inside another (E023 — only `{- -}` nests). Each names the delimiter at fault and how to close it.
-- **E024** — A source file that is not UTF-8: the byte that does not decode, its offset, line and column, and the `iconv` command that converts the file to UTF-8 (an imported module's E024 is located in the module)
-- **E030–E032** — Contract syntax: an `old()`/`new()` argument that is not an effect reference (E030, E031), or a contract clause written after `effects` (E032)
-- **E040** — A pipe whose right operand is not a call: `a |> b` needs `b` to be a call with an argument list, such as `a |> f()`
-- **E010** — Transform errors (internal)
-- **E1xx** — Type check: core + expressions (type mismatches, slot resolution, operators, declarations, termination)
-- **E2xx** — Type check: calls (unresolved functions, argument mismatches, module calls, ability operations)
-- **E3xx** — Type check: control flow (if/match, patterns, effect handlers)
-- **E5xx** — Verification (contract violations, undecidable fallbacks, primitive-operation safety incl. arithmetic overflow, premise satisfiability, and E541: a runtime-check claim `vera verify` found no check for in the compiled module)
-- **E6xx** — Codegen (unsupported features, name collisions, typed holes block compilation); **E699** is an internal compiler error
-- **E7xx** — Testing (contract violations, input generation, execution errors, a proof a test run refutes)
-- **E8xx** — Run: a program's own failure while it runs (**E800**, a runtime trap: its `trap_kind`, the source backtrace and the kind's fix)
-- **E9xx** — Command: the command line's own refusals, not a property of the program (a file not found, an option a command does not take or a value it does not accept, a function `--fn` cannot call, arguments that do not fit the function, a port in use, a missing optional dependency, an output path that cannot be written)

-- `Int` — signed 64-bit integer; arithmetic overflow traps (and `INT_MIN / -1` traps with no verifier obligation)
-- `Nat` — natural number, the non-negative half of the 64-bit `Int` (`0` to `2^63 - 1`)

-- `Byte` — unsigned 8-bit integer (0–255)

 ### When to use recursion instead
 
 Closures cover pure, self-contained transformations and simple captured constants. Prefer a top-level recursive function when any of these hold:
 
-- The body needs an effect row other than `pure` that doesn't match the combinator's expected effect signature.
-- The body needs to early-return or short-circuit in a way the combinator doesn't provide (`array_find` / `array_any` / `array_all` short-circuit; `array_map` / `array_fold` do not).
-- The iteration shape isn't one-pass left-to-right (e.g. you need to look ahead, or process in reverse while mutating a different data structure).
-- Termination requires a `decreases` clause that proves non-trivial progress — closures cannot carry `decreases`.

 ## What are abilities?
 
-Abilities are Vera's mechanism for constrained generics — type constraints that restrict what types a generic function can accept. They're inspired by Roc's ability system and serve a similar role to Haskell's type classes or Rust's traits, but with a fixed set of built-in abilities rather than user-defined ones.

They are inspired by Roc's ability system and serve a similar role to Haskell's type classes or Rust's traits, but with a fixed set of built-in abilities rather than user-defined ones.
 
 Vera has four built-in abilities:
 
-- **`Eq<T>`** — equality comparison via `eq(a, b)`, satisfied by all primitive types and ADTs whose fields are themselves `Eq`
-- **`Ord<T>`** — ordering via `compare(a, b)`, which returns the built-in `Ordering` ADT (`Less`, `Equal`, `Greater`), satisfied by `Int`, `Nat`, `Bool`, `Float64`, `String`, and `Byte`
-- **`Hash<T>`** — hashing via `hash(x)`, which returns an `Int`, satisfied by `Int`, `Nat`, `Bool`, `Float64`, `String`, and `Byte`
-- **`Show<T>`** — string conversion via `show(x)`, satisfied by `Int`, `Nat`, `Bool`, `Float64`, `String`, and `Byte`

 ## How does HTTP work in Vera?
 
 HTTP is modelled as a built-in algebraic effect. `Http.get(url)` and `Http.post(url, body)` are effect operations that return `Result<String, String>`. Functions that use them must declare `effects(<Http>)` in their signature, making network access explicit and trackable in the type system.

The pattern for fetching and parsing JSON from an API is: call `Http.get`, then `json_parse` the response body.

 ## How does contract-driven testing work?
 
-`vera test` is Vera's built-in testing command. It generates test inputs automatically from function contracts — you don't write test cases manually.
+`vera test` is Vera's built-in testing command. It generates test inputs from function contracts, so you do not write test cases by hand.
 
-![Contract-driven testing: Z3 generates inputs satisfying each requires clause, every input runs for real as WASM under wasmtime, and the ensures postcondition is checked against the actual output — a violation fails with the concrete input.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aallan/vera/main/assets/diagrams/contract-testing.svg)

Proved functions run only under --distrust.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aallan/vera/main/assets/diagrams/contract-testing.svg)
 
 The process works in three steps:
 
-1. **Input generation**: The compiler reads each function's `requires()` clause and uses Z3 to generate concrete values that satisfy the precondition. For example, if a function requires `@Int.1 != 0`, Z3 produces pairs of integers where the first is non-zero — `@Int.1` is the leftmost parameter, since De Bruijn indices count back from the most recent binding. It generates up to 100 trials per function by default (configurable with `--trials`). Whether a parameter can be generated for is decided on its *resolved* type, not its spelling, so an alias of a generatable type (`type Cnt = Int;`) is trialled rather than skipped, and an alias-spelled precondition still constrains the inputs. "Satisfy the precondition" is exact rather than best-effort, for the functions that reach trials at all: among the Tier-3 targets, if any conjunct — or any refined parameter's predicate — falls outside the SMT layer's decidable fragment, Z3 cannot constrain the inputs by it, so the function is *skipped* with the blocking conjunct named instead of being exercised on inputs its own guard would reject. A function the verifier proved at Tier 1 is reported `VERIFIED` and never trialled, so the question does not arise for it — unless `vera test --distrust` runs it too, and then a proved function whose precondition the generator cannot honour is reported `VERIFIED` and not exercised, never run on inputs its precondition does not admit.

 ## Why WebAssembly?
 
-Three reasons. First, portability — the same `.wasm` module runs at the command line and in the browser, which is what the browser-parity suite asserts by running identical module bytes under both hosts; `--target wasi-p2` emits a WASI 0.2 component from that same source. Second, sandboxing — WebAssembly has no ambient capabilities, so a Vera program cannot do anything its effect declarations don't permit. Third, the WASM Component Model (W3C, production-ready in Wasmtime) will enable Vera components to interoperate with Rust, Go, and Python components via WIT interfaces, providing ecosystem access without requiring a massive native package system.

-- **A precondition refuted only over a stand-in is checked at run time, in every position.**  A user function's precondition that cannot be proven at a call because an argument is a stand-in is a check the compiled program makes where it evaluates it ([#1480](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1480)) — in the function body as in a `requires`, an `ensures`, a `decreases` measure or a refinement predicate, or at a call only the verifier's obligation walk reaches (in an argument of a built-in the verifier does not model, in an interpolated part, in a `handle` body), and for a built-in's declared domain at any call.  A precondition refuted only over a stand-in, one that some value of the stand-in satisfies, takes the **E532** Tier-3 demotion above, with that check behind it; one false for every value the stand-in could take is **E501**; and an `assume` about the value discharges either. A call precondition over a binder of a closure, of a quantifier's predicate or of a handler clause, which the verifier reads without its value, is E532 as well, as an argument that does not translate is.  A value is unknown only as far as its binder's type leaves it: code generation guards the bind of a binder declared at a refinement type before anything in its scope runs (Section 2.6.5), so the verifier takes the binder's predicate as a fact about it, and a precondition that predicate entails is discharged — `need_pos(@Pos.0)` after `let @Pos = get(())`, or in a `Some(@Pos)` arm whether or not the scrutinee translates, verifies, and a violating value traps at the bind.  Under a scrutinee that translates, the binder would read the projection its own bind is obligated over, so it is bound to a fresh value equal to that projection, and only a goal that reads the fresh value is given the predicate: the bind's obligation stays the runtime guard.  The predicate is given on the runs where the bind runs — the arm's own pattern matched and no earlier arm's did, and the same of every arm and branch enclosing the `match` — and on no others: in the verifier's translation of the `match`, whose value can carry the binder past the arm, the binder of an arm whose pattern holds a `String` literal inside a constructor, a test that translation does not state, is the projection and carries nothing. -**String length** ([#802](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/802)).  Vera strings are UTF-8 byte sequences and `string_length` returns the **byte** count, but Z3's string theory (SMT-LIB 2.6) models strings as sequences of Unicode **code points** — its `Length` counts code points, which disagrees with the runtime on every multibyte character (`string_length("é")` is `2`, not `1`).  `string_length` is therefore modeled at **Tier 1** only for a string **literal**, whose exact byte length is known; on any non-literal argument it defers to a runtime-guarded **Tier 3** obligation (Z3's string theory has no byte-length operator).  The boolean predicates `string_contains` / `string_starts_with` / `string_ends_with` stay **Tier 1**: UTF-8 is self-synchronizing, so a valid substring / prefix / suffix matches at the byte level exactly when it matches at the code-point level.  The other byte/offset-sensitive string builtins (`string_slice`, `string_index_of`, `string_char_code`, `string_chars`) are not translated to Z3 and already fall to **Tier 3**.  Two further deferrals keep the predicates honest.  Z3's string-sort alphabet only reaches U+2FFFF, and its Python binding silently stores any higher code point as the literal's *escape text* rather than the character — so a literal containing a code point **above U+2FFFF** is unusable in the `z3.StringVal`-based predicate translation (`string_contains` / `string_starts_with` / `string_ends_with`) and defers to **Tier 3** there, instead of letting a predicate match phantom escape bytes the runtime never sees.  `string_length` is unaffected by this one — it byte-counts the *decoded* literal, so an astral literal's length stays **Tier 1**.  A **lone surrogate** (U+D800–U+DFFF) defers on **both** paths: `z3.StringVal` stores it as phantom escape text just like the astral case, and — since it has no UTF-8 encoding at all — `string_length`'s byte count cannot be taken either.

Three Float64 builtins are modeled at **Tier 1**.  `float_clamp(v, lo, hi)` is pure Float64 and modeled **unconditionally** as the faithful WASM `f64.min(f64.max(v, lo), hi)` — NaN-propagating and ±0-correct. -**Refinement predicates at a call argument** (§2.6.4).  A refinement the caller must establish is obligated wherever the value enters a refined slot, and that includes the refinements a parameter's type writes on a **component** — an ADT payload, a tuple component.  Those are *assumed* by the callee, which is verified once for every caller, so the value's own positions must establish them — the argument (a closure's included), a `let` binder, a constructor field, a tuple component, an effect-operation argument, and the function's return slot, the last of which is what makes the rule transitive.  A construction is excluded only where its own site carries the obligation.  The discharge is a solver query with the source's component invariants as premises, withheld when that source's producer was disclosed.  The tiering follows the guard rather than the site — the boundary guard reaches a parameter's own refinement and its tuple components only (§2.6.5), so an undischarged payload or array-element obligation is `tier3_unguarded`/`E506` while an undischarged tuple-component one is a guarded Tier 3.

-Built-in functions are always in scope as the single canonical definition of each operation. +          } else {
+            None
+          };
+          match @Option<Int>.0 {
+            Some(@Int) -> @Int.0,
+            None -> 0
+          }
+        }
+        """),
+    "an array literal": MAG + textwrap.dedent("""\
+        public fn f(@Int -> @Int)
+          requires(true)
+          ensures(@Int.result >= 0)
+          effects(pure)
+        {
+          let @Array<Int> = [mag(@Int.0)];
+          @Array<Int>.0[0]
+        }
+        """),
+    "a refined parameter boxed": POS + BOX + textwrap.dedent("""\
+        public fn f(@PosInt -> @Int)
+          requires(true)
+          ensures(@Int.result > 0)
+          effects(pure)
+        {
+          let @Box = MkBox(@PosInt.0);
+          match @Box.0 {
+            MkBox(@Int) -> @Int.0
+          }
+        }
+        """),
+    "a refined return boxed": POS + BOX + textwrap.dedent("""\
+        private fn pos(@Int -> @PosInt)
+          requires(@Int.0 > 0)
+          ensures(true)
+          effects(pure)
+        {
+          @Int.0
+        }
+
+        public fn f(@Int -> @Int)
+          requires(@Int.0 > 0)
+          ensures(@Int.result > 0)
+          effects(pure)
+        {
+          let @Box = MkBox(pos(@Int.0));
+          match @Box.0 {
+            MkBox(@Int) -> @Int.0
+          }
+        }
+        """),
+    "a Nat parameter boxed": BOX + textwrap.dedent("""\
+        public fn f(@Nat -> @Int)
+          requires(true)
+          ensures(@Int.result >= 0)
+          effects(pure)
+        {
+          let @Box = MkBox(@Nat.0);
+          match @Box.0 {
+            MkBox(@Int) -> @Int.0
+          }
+        }
+        """),
+}
+
+#: Programs the same field read must NOT prove.
+CONTROLS: dict[str, str] = {
+    "a postcondition stronger than the fact": BOX + MAG + textwrap.dedent("""\
+        public fn f(@Int -> @Int)
+          requires(true)
+          ensures(@Int.result > 0)
+          effects(pure)
+        {
+          let @Box = MkBox(mag(@Int.0));
+          match @Box.0 {
+            MkBox(@Int) -> @Int.0
+          }
+        }
+        """),
+    "a field holding a value no contract speaks of": BOX + textwrap.dedent("""\
+        public fn f(@Int -> @Int)
+          requires(true)
+          ensures(@Int.result >= 0)
+          effects(pure)
+        {
+          let @Box = MkBox(@Int.0);
+          match @Box.0 {
+            MkBox(@Int) -> @Int.0
+          }
+        }
+        """),
+    "the other field of a nested constructor": NESTED + MAG + textwrap.dedent("""\
+        public fn f(@Int -> @Int)
+          requires(true)
+          ensures(@Int.result >= 0)
+          effects(pure)
+        {
+          let @Outer = MkOuter(MkPair(mag(@Int.0), -7));
+          match @Outer.0 {
+            MkOuter(MkPair(@Int, @Int)) -> @Int.0
+          }
+        }
+        """),
+    "a box from a callee whose contract is ensures(true)": BOX + MAG + textwrap.dedent("""\
+        private fn wrap(@Int -> @Box)
+          requires(true)
+          ensures(true)
+          effects(pure)
+        {
+          MkBox(mag(@Int.0))
+        }
+
+        public fn f(@Int -> @Int)
+          requires(true)
+          ensures(@Int.result >= 0)
+          effects(pure)
+        {
+          match wrap(@Int.0) {
+            MkBox(@Int) -> @Int.0
+          }
+        }
+        """),
+}
+
+
+def _ensures(source: str, fn: str) -> tuple[list[str], list[str]]:
+    """The statuses of *fn*'s `ensures` obligations in *source*, and the
+    codes of the run's error diagnostics."""
+    result = _verify(source)
+    statuses = [o.status for o in result.obligations
+                if o.kind == "ensures" and o.fn_name == fn]
+    errors = [d.error_code for d in result.diagnostics
+              if d.severity == "error"]
+    return statuses, errors
+
+
+def test_repro_box_then_unbox_proves() -> None:
+    """The program #909 filed: `MkBox(mag(-5))` matched back proves
+    `ensures(@Int.result >= 0)` on `main`."""
+    statuses, errors = _ensures(REPRO, "main")
+    assert statuses == ["verified"]
+    assert errors == []
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("shape", sorted(SHAPES))
+def test_fact_holds_through_a_field(shape: str) -> None:
+    statuses, errors = _ensures(SHAPES[shape], "f")
+    assert statuses == ["verified"], shape
+    assert errors == [], shape
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("control", sorted(CONTROLS))
+def test_field_read_proves_nothing_the_fact_does_not(control: str) -> None:
+    statuses, errors = _ensures(CONTROLS[control], "f")
+    assert statuses == ["violated"], control
+    assert errors == ["E500"], control
+
+
+# =====================================================================
+# The callee in another module
+# =====================================================================
+
+#: `mag`, exported by a module of its own.
+MAGNITUDE = "module magnitude;\n\n" + MAG.replace(
+    "private fn mag", "public fn mag")
+
+_IMPORTER = "import magnitude(mag);\n\n" + BOX + textwrap.dedent("""\
+    public fn f(@Int -> @Int)
+      requires(true)
+      ensures(POST)
+      effects(pure)
+    {
+      let @Box = MkBox(CALL);
+      match @Box.0 {
+        MkBox(@Int) -> @Int.0
+      }
+    }
+    """)
+
+
+def _imported(tmp_path: Path, call: str, post: str) -> tuple[list[str], list[str]]:
+    """The statuses of `f`'s `ensures` and the error codes, where `f` boxes
+    *call*, a call of the imported `mag`, and promises *post*."""
+    assert "public fn mag" in MAGNITUDE
+    files = {
+        "magnitude.vera": MAGNITUDE,
+        "main.vera": _IMPORTER.replace("CALL", call).replace("POST", post),
+    }
+    _diagnostics, result = verify_multi_module(tmp_path, files)
+    statuses = [o.status for o in result.obligations
+                if o.kind == "ensures" and o.fn_name == "f"]
+    errors = [d.error_code for d in result.diagnostics
+              if d.severity == "error"]
+    return statuses, errors
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("call", ["mag(@Int.0)", "magnitude::mag(@Int.0)"])
+def test_fact_from_an_imported_callee_holds_through_a_field(
+    tmp_path: Path, call: str,
+) -> None:
+    statuses, errors = _imported(tmp_path, call, "@Int.result >= 0")
+    assert statuses == ["verified"], call
+    assert errors == [], call
+
+
+def test_imported_callee_proves_nothing_its_contract_does_not(

+) -> None:

+    assert errors == ["E500"]

problem_statement.title: Verifier: a value's postcondition/refinement is not propagated through an ADT field (box then unbox loses the fact)
problem_statement.body:
## Summary

A verifier **incompleteness** (not a soundness bug): a value's postcondition or refinement is not propagated **through an ADT field**. When a provably-constrained value is stored into a `data` constructor field and later recovered with `match`, the constraint is forgotten, so a postcondition whose truth depends on that constraint cannot be discharged at Tier 1.

This is conservative — the verifier never *proves* a false property; it only fails to prove some *true* ones (and the contract is still enforced at runtime).

## Reproduction

```vera
private data Box { MkBox(Int) }

private fn mag(@Int -> @Int)
  requires(true) ensures(@Int.result >= 0) effects(pure)   -- mag GUARANTEES result >= 0
{ if @Int.0 < 0 then { 0 - @Int.0 } else { @Int.0 } }

public fn main(@Unit -> @Int)
  requires(true) ensures(@Int.result >= 0) effects(pure)   -- TRUE: the field can only come from mag
{
  let @Box = MkBox(mag(-5));               -- box a provably->=0 value
  match @Box.0 { MkBox(@Int) -> @Int.0 }   -- unbox and return it
}
```

```
$ vera check  main.vera    # OK
$ vera verify main.vera    # Cannot statically verify postcondition in 'main'. Function body
                           # uses constructs outside the decidable fragment. Contract will be
                           # checked at runtime.  ->  3 verified (Tier 1), 2 runtime checks (Tier 3)
$ vera run    main.vera    # 5   (mag(-5) = 5 >= 0 — the Tier-3 runtime check passes)
```

`main`'s postcondition `result >= 0` is genuinely true (the field can only have been produced by `mag`), but the `>= 0` fact attached to `mag`'s result is dropped the moment it is stored into `MkBox`'s field and recovered by `match`. The unboxed value is treated as an arbitrary `Int`, so the obligation cannot be discharged at Tier 1 and **degrades to a Tier-3 runtime check** (on some program shapes it instead surfaces as an unprovable obligation / counterexample rather than a demotion — same underlying gap).

## Why this is a limitation, not a bug

- **Sound**: the verifier never proves a false property. The *false* variant (`ensures(@Int.result > 0)`, which is not always true here) is still correctly rejected, and the contract is enforced at runtime. Full postcondition/refinement propagation through arbitrary data structures is undecidable in general; Vera's verifier degrades gracefully to Tier 3 (DESIGN.md: "degrades gracefully where SMT is undecidable").
- **Not module-specific**: reproduces identically with a same-file callee (`mag` above) and a cross-module callee (a module `magnitude` boxed then unboxed), confirming it is a general ADT-field fact-propagation gap, not a codegen or module-resolution issue.

Same family as the verifier reporting/completeness gaps #764, #776, #779 (statically-obligated-elsewhere or runtime-guarded; the program never does the wrong thing).

## Workarounds

- Give the field a refinement type so the constraint travels with it, or
- re-establish the fact after unboxing (an explicit narrowing / assertion), or
- accept the Tier-3 runtime check, which enforces the contract dynamically.

## Provenance

Surfaced by the adversarial review of PR #907 (observation N2). Pre-existing; the verifier stage is untouched by that PR.

problem_statement.title: gql: execute() leaves its event processor on the isolation scope, so later unrelated errors are reported as GraphQL requests
problem_statement.body:
### How do you use Sentry?

Sentry Saas (sentry.io)

### Version

master (860a060), gql 4.4.0

### Steps to Reproduce

`sentry_patched_execute` adds an event processor to the isolation scope on every `Client.execute()` and never removes it:

```python
scope = sentry_sdk.get_isolation_scope()
scope.add_event_processor(_make_gql_event_processor(self, document))
```

gql is a client, so it's often called outside a per-request isolation scope (scripts, workers, task loops), or many times inside one request. The processors outlive the query and apply to every later event on that scope.

```python
import sentry_sdk
from gql import Client, gql
from gql.transport.requests import RequestsHTTPTransport
from sentry_sdk.integrations.gql import GQLIntegration

sentry_sdk.init(dsn=..., integrations=[GQLIntegration()], send_default_pii=True)
client = Client(transport=RequestsHTTPTransport(url="http://example.com/graphql"))

for i in range(100):
    client.execute(gql("query Q%d { example }" % i))  # all succeed

# later, unrelated to GraphQL
try:
    raise ValueError("unrelated error")
except ValueError:
    sentry_sdk.capture_exception()
```

Full repro (HTTP mocked with `responses`, events captured from a custom transport): https://github.com/Mohil-Ahuja/ci-scratch/blob/main/repro/gql_processors.py, run output: https://github.com/Mohil-Ahuja/ci-scratch/actions/runs/42837565235

### Expected Result

The unrelated `ValueError` has no GraphQL request data, and `contexts.response.type` is `"response"` on gql error events.

### Actual Result

1. **Unrelated errors are tagged as GraphQL requests.** The `ValueError` above is sent with the last query attached:

   ```json
   "request": {"api_target": "graphql", "method": "POST", "url": "http://example.com/graphql",
               "data": {"query": "query Q99 {\n  example\n}", "variables": null, "operationName": "Q99"}}
   ```

2. **Other processors on the scope get wiped.** Once a scope has more than 20 processors, `Scope.add_event_processor` clears all of them. So 21 gql calls in one request remove processors added by the app or other integrations. In the repro, a processor added to the same isolation scope before 21 queries is gone afterwards, and the next error event is missing its tag.

3. **`contexts.response.type` is a self-reference.** Both branches of the processor do `response.update({"data": ..., "type": response})`, which sets `type` to the dict itself, so it's serialized as `"<cyclic>"`:

   ```json
   "response": {"data": {"errors": [{"message": "boom"}]}, "type": "<cyclic>"}
   ```

Possible fix: fork a scope around `real_execute` (`with sentry_sdk.new_scope() as scope:`) and add the processor there, so it only applies to events captured during the query (including the `TransportQueryError` event), and set `"type": "response"`. Happy to open a PR with tests.

problem_statement.title: Non-idempotent output with `profile = "black"`: `from X import a as b, Z` needs two runs, so `isort --check` fails after `isort`
problem_statement.body:
### Summary
When a single from import mixes a plain name with an as alias, and the alias import has to wrap, the first isort run leaves the plain-name import on one line. A second run then rewrites it as a parenthesised multi-line import.

As a result, isort --check-only fails on a file that isort has just formatted.
### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create `pyproject.toml`:
 ```toml
   [tool.isort]
   profile = "black"
   line_length = 40
   ```
2. Create `t.py` containing one line:
 ```python
   from requests import long_name_here as long_name_here2, Z
   ```
3. Run:
 ```
   isort t.py
   isort --check-only --diff t.py; echo "exit code: $?"
   ```
### Expected Behaviour:
The output of the first run is stable, so the second command passes with exit code 0.
### Actual Behaviour:
The first command prints `Fixing .../t.py`. The second reports `Imports are incorrectly sorted and/or formatted.` and exits with code 1:
```diff
-from requests import Z
+from requests import (
+    Z,
+)
 from requests import (
     long_name_here as long_name_here2,
 )
```
A third run changes nothing, so the output settles after two runs, but only after the first run's output has been rejected.
### Environment
- isort 10.0.0b3 
- Branch: main
- Commit: 841e43126cd2ca74751b421afd00d90ca36932e5
- Python 3.14.4
- Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS (WSL)
### Notes
- I only varied `line_length`. 
- This appears related to [#2352](https://github.com/PyCQA/isort/issues/2352), which reported non-idempotent formatting involving aliased and directly imported names. That issue was closed after the behaviour was reported fixed on main. However, I can still reproduce similar behaviour on isort 10.0.0b3.
- This looks related to, but distinct from, #2694 (comments on names hoisted to the `(` line), #2741 (comment lost on `X as X` re-exports).My reproduction contains no comments.
- I haven't traced the cause. My guess is that the first pass decides whether to wrap `from requests import Z` using the original combined line, and the second pass decides differently on the already-split line. I haven't verified that.
- Happy to try a fix and open a PR if that would help.

+def _group_ncs_files_into_streams(folder_path: DirectoryPath) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
+    """
+    Group the `.ncs` files of a Neuralynx folder into neo's streams by reading their headers only.
+
+    The streams and their names follow ``NeuralynxRawIO._parse_header``: channels share a stream when they share
+    sampling rate, input range and DSP filter settings, streams are numbered from the highest sampling rate down,
+    and the filter number is the position of the stream's filter settings among the sorted distinct ones. Unlike
+    neo, the timestamps are not read, so the folder is grouped even when its streams have gaps at different times.
+
+    Returns
+    -------
+    dict[str, list[str]]
+        The names of the `.ncs` files of each stream, keyed by stream name.
+    """
+    from neo.rawio import NeuralynxRawIO
+    from neo.rawio.neuralynxrawio.nlxheader import NlxHeader
+
+    file_paths = sorted((path for path in Path(folder_path).iterdir() if path.is_file()), key=lambda path: path.name)
+    ncs_file_paths = [path for path in file_paths if path.suffix.lower() == ".ncs"]
+
+    file_names_per_stream_key = {}
+    for file_path in ncs_file_paths:
+        # neo skips files that hold only a header
+        if file_path.stat().st_size <= NlxHeader.HEADER_SIZE:
+            continue
+        header = NlxHeader(str(file_path))
+        for channel_index in range(len(header["channel_ids"])):
+            input_range = header.get("InputRange")
+            if isinstance(input_range, list):
+                input_range = input_range[channel_index] if channel_index < len(input_range) else input_range[0]
+            filter_parameters = tuple(
+                sorted((key, header[key]) for key in NeuralynxRawIO._filter_keys if key in header)
+            )
+            stream_key = (float(header["sampling_rate"]), input_range, filter_parameters)
+            file_names = file_names_per_stream_key.setdefault(stream_key, [])
+            if file_path.name not in file_names:
+                file_names.append(file_path.name)
+
+    filter_number = {
+        filter_parameters: number
+        for number, filter_parameters in enumerate(sorted({stream_key[2] for stream_key in file_names_per_stream_key}))
+    }
+    stream_keys = sorted(file_names_per_stream_key, reverse=True, key=lambda stream_key: stream_key[0])
+
+    file_names_per_stream = {}
+    for stream_index, (sampling_rate, input_range, filter_parameters) in enumerate(stream_keys):
+        input_range_mv = int(input_range / 1000) if input_range is not None else 0
+        stream_name = (
+            f"stream{stream_index}_{int(sampling_rate)}Hz_{input_range_mv}mVRange"
+            f"_DSPFilter{filter_number[filter_parameters]}"
+        )
+        file_names_per_stream[stream_name] = file_names_per_stream_key[(sampling_rate, input_range, filter_parameters)]
+    return file_names_per_stream
+

problem_statement.title: [Bug]: `NeuralynxRecordingInterface` fails on Neuralynx data with multiple streams
problem_statement.body:
### What happened?

When trying to convert a Neuralynx dataset following the snippet from the [conversion gallery](https://neuroconv.readthedocs.io/en/main/conversion_examples_gallery/recording/neuralynx.html), the initialization of `NeuralynxRecordingInterface()` fails if the dataset contains channels (`.ncs` files) from multiple streams, that is groups of recording channels that have different sampling rates.

To my understanding, `NeuralynxRecordingInterface` relies on the [`_NeoBaseExtractor.get_neo_io_reader(**neo_kwargs)`](https://github.com/SpikeInterface/spikeinterface/blob/d963aa26e31a9b6bc0bea2a4973f76d4dbafb062/src/spikeinterface/extractors/neoextractors/neobaseextractor.py#L43) from the `spikeinterface` package which propagates `**neo_kwargs` to the dedicated neo reader. And neo readers allow the `exclude_filename` argument (see [NeuralynxRawIO](https://neo.readthedocs.io/en/latest/rawiolist.html#neo.rawio.NeuralynxRawIO)) where the user can choose to exclude offending recording channels. However, `NeuralynxRecordingInterface()` does not expect the `exclude_filename` parameter.

Currently, `NeuralynxRecordingInterface` allows the `stream_name` parameter, but that will fail too since it goes via the above `.get_neo_io_reader()` method of the spikeinterface package.

## Possible fix
Allow `NeuralynxRecordingInterface` to accept `exclude_filename` keyword argument.

The current workaround is to simply do conversion separately for groups of channels with different sampling rates (i.e. put them in separate folders). If i understand correctly, would lead to several *.nwb files (one for each stream). I don't know if that's a desired behavior or if the NWB standard allows different sampling rates per dataset. 

### Steps to Reproduce
For example, in MNE-Python testing data we have a small (< 1MB) [Neuralynx testing dataset](https://github.com/mne-tools/mne-testing-data/tree/master/neuralynx) with one channel sampled at 2kHz (`LAHC1.ncs`) and another one at 32kHz (`LAHCu1.ncs`).

If I place those two channels into the same folder and run this code I get the traceback pasted below:

```python
from neuroconv.datainterfaces import NeuralynxRecordingInterface
folder_path = "/path/to/testing/dataset"

# this fails with the traceback below
interface = NeuralynxRecordingInterface(folder_path=folder_path, verbose=False)
```

problem_statement.title: BUG: CholeskyCorr(upper=True) returns a lower-triangular factor
problem_statement.body:
### Describe the issue:

`CholeskyCorrTransform(n=3, upper=True)` returns a lower-triangular factor. For unconstrained `[0.2, -0.4, 0.8]` the strictly upper part is `[0, 0, 0]` and the strictly lower part is `[0.196116, 0, 0.624695]`. A caller who reads the upper triangle gets zero correlations.

### Reproduceable code example:

```python
import numpy as np
import pytensor.tensor as pt
from pymc.distributions.transforms import CholeskyCorrTransform

z = np.array([0.2, -0.4, 0.8])
factor = CholeskyCorrTransform(n=3, upper=True).backward(pt.as_tensor(z)).eval()
print(factor)
print("strictly lower", factor[np.tril_indices(3, k=-1)])
print("strictly upper", factor[np.triu_indices(3, k=1)])
```

```
[[1.         0.         0.        ]
 [0.19611614 0.98058068 0.        ]
 [0.         0.62469505 0.78086881]]
strictly lower [0.19611614 0.         0.62469505]
strictly upper [0. 0. 0.]
```

The default `upper=False` path is lower-triangular, as documented.

### Error message:

None. The factor is finite and has unit diagonal.

### PyMC version information:

```
PyMC: 6.3.2+21.gd1a761e84
PyTensor: 3.3.0
Python: 3.12.10
Operating system: macOS arm64
Install: editable checkout of d1a761e84
```

### Context for the issue:

`CholeskyCorrTransform.__init__` says `upper=True` transforms to an upper triangular matrix and `upper=False` to a lower triangular matrix. The padding always builds a lower triangle; the flag does not change the returned triangle. A correlation prior requested in upper-triangular Cholesky form is stored as the transpose, so every correlation read from the upper triangle is zero.

Expected behavior: with `upper=True` the strictly lower part is zero and the correlations sit in the upper triangle.

problem_statement.title: [Regridder] Support regridding to HEALPix target grids
problem_statement.body:
### Feature request

AQUA can regrid to regular grids by AQUA name (`r100`) or by CDO name (`r360x180`). HEALPix target grids should work the same way: CDO supports them (`hp<nside>_nested`, `hpr<zoom>`), and smmregrid already recognises these names in `CdoGrid`. Today they fail unless the **source** grid is also HEALPix.

Tested on CI data (smmregrid 0.3.0, CDO 2.6.6), target zoom level 3 nested (`hp8_nested` / `hpr3`):

| Source | Result |
|---|---|
| IFS `test-tco79` | ❌ weights generation fails |
| FESOM `test-pi` | ❌ weights generation fails |
| ICON `test-healpix` | ✅ works |

CDO stops while generating the conservative weights:

    cdo gencon (Warning): HEALPix cell edges are not located on great circles. This leads to inaccuracies in the calculation of cell areas.
    cdo gencon (Abort): Use the CDO option --force to perform this operation.

ICON works only because its source grid (`test-healpix`) sets `cdo_options: "--force"`.

**What is missing in AQUA**

1. `Regridder.weights()` passes only the source grid's `cdo_options` to smmregrid. The target grid's `cdo_options` are ignored. As a result, even AQUA's own file-based HEALPix grids (e.g. `hpz3-nested`, which sets `--force`) fail as a target.
2. A HEALPix grid given as a CDO name has no grid dictionary, so nothing can set `--force` for it.

**Proposed change (AQUA only, no smmregrid release needed)**

- `GridDictHandler`: when the grid is a HEALPix CDO name, add `cdo_options: "--force"` to its grid dictionary.
- `Regridder.weights()`: pass the target grid's `cdo_options` too (merged with the source's, duplicates dropped).

A prototype passes `tests/test_regrid.py`. With it, IFS and FESOM regrid to `hp8_nested` / `hpr3`, and the output cell centres match healpy (nested ordering) to 5e-11°.

**Possible follow-ups in smmregrid (later release)**

- Add `--force` automatically in `CdoGenerate` when the source or target is a HEALPix CDO name. The AQUA-side `GridDictHandler` change could then be removed.
- Recognise the `healpix_index` dimension, which CDO 2.6 writes for the deprecated `hpzN` names, in `GridInspector`.
- smmregrid always names an unstructured target dimension `cell`. Grid files that use another name (`cells` in `hpz3_nested_atm.nc`) then give a target area that doesn't match the regridded data, and `fldmean` fails.

problem_statement.title: An env specific --override with += drops the value inherited from [testenv]
problem_statement.body:
With a tox.ini like this:

    [tox]
    env_list = a
    [testenv]
    deps = x

running `tox config -e a -k deps -x testenv:a.deps+=zzz` prints `deps = zzz`. I expected `x` and `zzz`, since += is meant to append to the value that is already configured. The same thing happens with set_env+= and pass_env+=, and with `env.a.deps+=zzz` against env_run_base in a tox.toml.

Appending through the base section works as the docs show (`testenv.deps+=zzz` gives x and zzz). It's only the env specific spelling that loses the inherited entries. The override is attached to the loader for `testenv:a`, which has no deps of its own, so it ends up as the whole value and never looks at `[testenv]`. A run started this way installs fewer dependencies than configured and nothing warns about it.

I found #3173, where inheriting from the base section was said to be intentional, but that was about plain overrides replacing a value. I'm not sure the same reasoning applies to +=, since append already says "keep what is there". If this is working as intended I'm happy to leave it. I have a fix ready (about 100 lines, mostly in loader/api.py and of_type.py, with tests for ini and toml) and can open a PR if you think it's worth having.

Checked on main at 7bd2f266.
